overview: East Prussia was a province of Germany. This atlas covers only 1920 to 1938, with incomplete outlines. Its longer history encompasses household skills and scientific inquiry, Nazi persecution, war and forced displacement.

periods.title: Earlier provincial background
periods.summary: After the 1772 partition of Poland, provincial arrangements changed repeatedly; East and West Prussia separated again in 1878.

periods.title: Separate province and urban change
periods.summary: East Prussia’s renewed separate provincial administration preceded the atlas window; towns expanded medical, transport and water infrastructure.

periods.title: The interwar province
periods.summary: East Prussia remained German but was geographically separated from the rest of Germany after the postwar settlement.

periods.title: Nazi rule and persecution
periods.summary: Jewish residents and political opponents lost rights and faced persecution and murder under National Socialism.

periods.title: Provincial end and forced displacement
periods.summary: War ended German provincial rule; partition, flight and expulsion transformed the region. Prussia itself was formally abolished in 1947.

sections.title: A province and an imperfect map

items.text: The 1920 outline contains Königsberg, Tilsit and Insterburg but omits Allenstein, now Olsztyn, and Elbing, now Elbląg; the 1930 outline includes those southern towns. Memel, now Klaipėda, and Danzig, now Gdańsk, lie outside both. These are coarse atlas snapshots, not reliable evidence that the omitted towns spent an entire decade outside East Prussia.

In 1772 Prussia annexed Warmia during the partition of Poland, incorporating it into East Prussia. From 1824 the eastern and western provinces shared a chief provincial administrator; they were separated again in 1878. The larger Prussian state had different borders.

After the First World War, East Prussia remained under German sovereignty but became separated from Germany’s main territory. Plebiscites helped settle southern and western boundaries in 1920. Olsztyn remained in Germany. A border vote decided state affiliation; it did not make every resident share one language or identity.

During the Weimar years, separation complicated trade while tourism brought visitors to the province. Its residents experienced both economic difficulties and opportunities associated with their landscape.

For a glimpse of a rural household in the 1920s and 1930s, the Olsztynek museum reconstructs an interior from Nowe Kawkowo. Its washing corner has a basin, water jug, towel and soap. Daily washing could happen in the kitchen, without a bathroom faucet. This is a museum reconstruction of a dated household setting.

Interwar rural laundry equipment included washboards and hand-operated washers. The museum’s examples include an expensive Miele machine with a wringer and a washing bell: a metal drum on a stick with a spring inside. Clean clothes required water, tools and muscle. There was no button that made the whole job disappear.

An 1880 butter churn from near Pisz survives in the Szczytno museum. Made of wood without nails, it rocks back and forth to turn cream into butter. The butter could then be shaped in carved wooden molds. Imagine finishing breakfast preparation with both a workout and a little edible sculpture.

The Szczytno museum’s exhibition, described in 2010, preserves tools of older Masurian food preparation: long troughs for kneading bread, cheese presses made from two boards, and containers whose names reflected their capacity. These objects illuminate inherited household skills; the exhibit does not date every utensil to the atlas’s 1920s.

The same retrospective collection follows linen from plant to clothing. Stems were broken to release fibers, combed, spun and woven; carved blocks could print patterns on finished cloth. This sequence shows why a household textile embodied many kinds of skilled labor long before anyone reached the ironing stage.

sections.title: Health, water and the toilet question

items.text: Olsztyn opened a modern hospital in 1867, before this atlas window, and gained a railway in 1872. By the interwar period residents inherited a town already changed by these nineteenth-century institutions. A hospital building tells us that organized medical care existed; it does not tell us that every family could obtain every treatment.

Olsztyn’s water company traces its 1893 waterworks project to epidemics of infectious disease. Earlier supplies came from wells and gravity-fed wooden pipes. Between 1927 and 1935 the pumping station and water-treatment equipment were rebuilt. Public health depended on maintained infrastructure as well as on what happened inside a doctor’s office.

Olsztyn’s sewer, operating from 1898, used the Welsh engineer Isaac Shone’s pneumatic system: compressed air pushed wastewater through pumping chambers. Yes, air pressure helped move the city’s sewage! The technology linked engineering with everyday cleanliness, rather than requiring every pipe to run conveniently downhill.

Surviving late nineteenth-century advertisements offered Olsztyn residents modern toilet equipment. Waterworks supported bathrooms and public baths, but coverage varied: the archive notes that Pisz still lacked a modern sewer enterprise in 1945. An indoor WC in a prosperous town home and a rural washing basin could belong to the same regional history.

On 28 April 1935, David Kaelter opened a Jewish school in Königsberg with 82 pupils, responding to Nazi exclusion from general education. Lessons included mathematics, grammar, Hebrew and Jewish history. An album now preserved at Yad Vashem contains photographs, drawings, stories and letters that help us see the children as individuals.

At this school in the mid-1930s, Friday gatherings brought children, teachers, parents and other community members together for songs, stories and pupils’ work. Letters also maintained friendships with children who had emigrated. Family and social life continued through deliberate acts of care during increasingly dangerous circumstances.

Polish-language schooling also mattered in the region. The Dom Gazety Olsztyńskiej museum documents Polish schools in Warmia and Masuria from 1929 to 1939 and their role in sustaining Polish identity. This is a specific educational history within the province, not evidence that all its schools taught in Polish.

A verified writing sample is “Gazeta Olsztyńska,” meaning “Olsztyn Newspaper,” printed on the masthead of issue 260 dated 6 November 1924. The language is Polish, using the Latin alphabet with diacritics; no separate transliteration is needed. This actual local newspaper is a small witness to Polish public writing inside German East Prussia.

At Rossitten on the Curonian Spit, Johannes Thienemann developed large-scale bird ringing from 1901, building on earlier work by the Danish teacher Hans Christian C. Mortensen. Marking birds made it possible to recognize individuals again and investigate migration. The atlas omits this thin coastal site, so this example belongs to the wider historical province.

In November 1938 Nazis burned the Königsberg synagogue and attacked the neighboring orphanage, driving children outside. Teachers were arrested. Schooling resumed under worsening conditions, but in 1942 the remaining pupils and parents were deported to Theresienstadt. Teacher Rosa Wolf stayed with her pupils and was murdered with them.

The Second World War ended East Prussia’s existence as a German province in 1945 amid destruction, civilian flight and subsequent expulsions. Southern East Prussia became part of Poland, while northern territory went to the Soviet Union. The end of an administration and the uprooting of communities were related events, but not the same thing.

Some displaced East Prussians rebuilt their lives in the Lüneburg area of Germany. In 1958 they established a museum devoted initially to hunting, forests and horses; its later remit widened. Such collections preserve memory outside the former province. They do not mean that the province continued as a state or territorial authority.

ending.text: The atlas stops at 1938; German provincial rule ended in 1945 amid partition and forced displacement. Prussia was abolished in 1947. Cultural memories continued beyond the province’s political existence.
